Given the assumed pivotal role of the medial EC (mEC) in controlling hippocampal activity,33,41,42 we examined whether and how optogenetic silencing of the mEC affects hippocampal SPW-Rs.
Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs) are critical for memory consolidation and retrieval. The neuronal content of spiking during SPW-Rs is believed to be under the influence of neocortical inputs via the entorhinal cortex (EC). Optogenetic silencing of the medial EC (mEC) reduced the incidence of SPW-Rs with minor impacts on their magnitude or duration, similar to local CA1 silencing.
The hippocampus is characterized by irregularly occurring sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs), most prevalent during non-REM (NREM) sleep.1 Hippocampal neuronal firing during SPW-Rs, particularly in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, is temporally organized, reflecting sequences that were expressed during past waking experiences.2,3,4,5 Owing to this exquisite feature of reactivating past experiences, SPW-Rs have been implicated with the consolidation of memory, and the transfer of information between the cortex and hippocampus.2,6 In support of this hypothesis, artificially truncating SPW-Rs leads to memory impairments,7,8,9,10 whereas the elongation of SPW-Rs improves memory.11 Therefore, the study of SPW-Rs and the neural mechanisms that generate such activity is highly relevant for behavior.
